summary: Small sensor signals often ride on large common-mode voltages. You see why a single op-amp difference amplifier loses its common-mode rejection to resistor tolerance, how the three-op-amp instrumentation amplifier fixes it, and design a load-cell front end with gain 100.
html:
The problem: a small difference on a large common voltage

A load-cell bridge (lesson 21) excited at 5 V produces a few millivolts between its two outputs, while both outputs sit near 2.5 V. Long cables also pick up mains hum equally on both wires. You want to amplify the differential voltage vd​=v2​−v1​ and reject the common-mode voltage vcm​=(v1​+v2​)/2.

The figure of merit is the common-mode rejection ratio: CMRR =Gd​/Gcm​, usually in dB. At CMRR = 100 dB, a 1 V common-mode signal looks like a 10 µV differential one.

The difference amplifier and its weakness

One op-amp with four resistors: v1​ through R1​ to the − input, R2​ as feedback, and v2​ through R3​ to the + input with R4​ to ground. With R2​/R1​=R4​/R3​, vout​=R1​R2​​(v2​−v1​), and in theory the common-mode gain is zero.

In practice, the ratios must match exactly. With resistor tolerance t, the worst-case CMRR is about

CMRR≈4t1+G​.

With 1 % resistors at unity gain, that’s only 50 (34 dB). It also loads the sources through R1​ and R3​.

The three-op-amp instrumentation amplifier

Two non-inverting buffers share a gain resistor RG​ between their inverting inputs, followed by a unity-gain difference amplifier.

  • The first stage amplifies the differential signal by 1+2R/RG​ but passes the common-mode signal at gain 1. So the CMRR improves by the first-stage gain before the mismatch-sensitive stage.
  • Both inputs see op-amp inputs: very high impedance.
  • One resistor, RG​, sets the gain. Integrated parts laser-trim the rest. For the classic AD620-style part: G=1+49.4 kΩ/RG​.

Datasheets give CMRR rising with gain, typically 90–130 dB at DC and falling with frequency, so 50 Hz hum is the true test.

Worked example

A load cell gives 2 mV/V at full scale with 5 V excitation, so 10 mV full scale. The cable picks up 1 V of 50 Hz common-mode hum.

  1. For about 1 V at full scale: G=100, so RG​=49.4 k/99=499 Ω (an E96 value), giving G=99.998.
  2. Full-scale output: 100×10 mV = 1.0 V.
  3. At 100 dB CMRR, the hum at the output is 100×1 V×10−5=1 mV, which is 0.1 % of full scale.
  4. A single difference amplifier with 1 % resistors at gain 100 would have CMRR ≈ 101/0.04=2525 (68 dB): the hum would be about 40 mV at the output, 4 % of full scale.

Code it from scratch

inamp.py
import itertools
import math

def diff_amp(v1, v2, R1, R2, R3, R4):
    return v2 * R4 / (R3 + R4) * (1 + R2 / R1) - v1 * R2 / R1

def cmrr_worst(G, tol, R=10e3):
    worst = math.inf
    for s in itertools.product((-1, 1), repeat=4):
        R1, R2, R3, R4 = (R * (1 + k * tol) * (G if i in (1, 3) else 1) for i, k in enumerate(s))
        gd = diff_amp(-0.5, 0.5, R1, R2, R3, R4)
        gcm = abs(diff_amp(1, 1, R1, R2, R3, R4))
        worst = min(worst, gd / gcm if gcm else math.inf)
    return worst

if __name__ == "__main__":
    assert abs(diff_amp(2.5, 2.51, 10e3, 10e3, 10e3, 10e3) - 0.01) < 1e-12
    c1 = cmrr_worst(1, 0.01)
    c100 = cmrr_worst(100, 0.01)
    print(f"difference amp, 1 % parts: CMRR {c1:.1f} ({20*math.log10(c1):.1f} dB) at G=1, {c100:.0f} at G=100")
    assert abs(c1 / (2 / 0.04) - 1) < 0.03 and abs(c100 / (101 / 0.04) - 1) < 0.03
    G = 1 + 49.4e3 / 499
    assert abs(G - 99.998) < 1e-3
    hum_out = G * 1.0 * 10 ** (-100 / 20)
    assert abs(hum_out - 1e-3) < 1e-6
    assert abs(G * 1.0 / c100 - 0.0396) < 0.002       # the plain difference amp lets ~40 mV through

Exercises

What RG​ gives a gain of 500 on the 49.4 kΩ in-amp? What’s the full-scale output for the 10 mV load cell?

Show the solution

RG​=49.4 k/499=99.0 Ω, so use 100 Ω (gain 495). Full scale: 4.95 V, too close to a 5 V rail; gain 300 would be safer.

Why does the in-amp’s first stage improve CMRR?

Show the solution

It amplifies the differential signal by 1+2R/RG​ but passes the common-mode signal at gain 1 (no current flows through RG​ when both inputs move together). The difference stage then sees a signal that’s already much larger relative to the common mode, so its mismatch matters less.
